title: Making your case
goals: Concede gracefully and then push back, using advanced concessives (Much as…, Try as they might, Be that as it may).
Handle albeit, notwithstanding, however + adjective and other concessive resources with their syntax and register.
Use the mandative subjunctive and fixed formulas (It is essential that he be…, Suffice it to say, Heaven forbid).
Build rhetorical parallelism: tricolon, anaphora, antithesis and correlatives without formal errors.
Refute courteously, identify fallacies (straw man, red herring, ad hominem) and attack arguments, not people.
Write and deliver a persuasive speech and rebuttal with precise debate vocabulary.

learn.title: Inverted concessives: Much as I…, Try as they might, Strange as it may seem
learn.html:
A rhetorical and formal structure for conceding something before opposing it: adjective / adverb / verb + as + subject + verb, followed by the main idea. It is equivalent to although, but with more force, since the conceded element is "brought forward" for dramatic effect.

PatternExampleMeaning
Much as + subject + verb of desire/appreciationMuch as I admire her courage, I can't endorse her plan.Although I admire her greatly…
Try as + subject + might / mayTry as they might, they could not close the gap.However hard they tried…
Adjective + as + subject + beBrilliant as the argument is, it rests on a false premise.However brilliant the argument is…
Adverb + as + subject + verbHard as she tried, she failed to persuade them.However hard she tried…
Strange as it may seemStrange as it may seem, the quietest speaker won.Odd as it may sound…
Noun + as + subject + be (literary)Child as she was, she grasped the stakes.Although she was only a child…
  • Inversion is obligatory: the concessive element goes first. Without that inversion, as means "while / because / as": As he spoke, we listened.
  • Interchangeable with though (Brilliant though it is…), but although does not allow this inversion: Although brilliant it is is an error.
  • No "but" or "yet": the main clause follows directly, just as with although.
  • Much as is used with verbs of feeling or desire (admire, like, enjoy, regret, want, wish) and with would like to: Much as I would like to help, my hands are tied.
  • Register: formal, oratorical. In spontaneous conversation as much as I… or although I… sounds more natural; in a speech, an essay or a debate, Much as… gives elegance and control.
  • Rhetorical effect: by conceding first, the speaker seems reasonable and has already "won over" the listener before contradicting them.

watch.wrong: Much as I like her, but I can't vote for her.
watch.right: Much as I like her, I can't vote for her.
watch.why: As with "although", "but" is not added: the main clause follows directly.

watch.right: Strange as it may seem, it works.
watch.why: The full formula is "Strange as it may seem"; the subject "it" is obligatory.

watch.wrong: As clever he is, he never listens.
watch.right: Clever as he is, he never listens.
watch.why: The adjective goes first, followed by "as": Clever as he is.

watch.wrong: Much as I would like helping you, I can't.
watch.right: Much as I would like to help you, I can't.
watch.why: "Would like" is followed by to + infinitive.

learn.title: Other concessives: Be that as it may, however + adjective, albeit, notwithstanding, for all
learn.html:
Each concessive resource has its own syntax, register and "direction". Mastering them lets you recognise the strength of your opponent's argument without giving up ground.

ResourceSyntaxExample and nuance
Be that as it mayFixed phrase that opens a sentenceBe that as it may, we must decide today. ("Regardless": accepts the previous point and moves on.)
However / no matter how + adj/adv + subject + verbFixed order: never However + subject + adjectiveHowever talented she is, she lacks discipline.
Whatever / whoever + nounClause with concessive valueWhatever the merits of the proposal, it will not pass.
albeit + adjective / adverb / short phraseDoes not introduce a full clause; very formalHe agreed, albeit reluctantly. / a modest, albeit significant, gain.
notwithstanding + nounFormal preposition; can follow the nounNotwithstanding these objections, the motion carried. / These objections notwithstanding, …
for all / with all + nounConcessive prepositionFor all her experience, she still made a basic error.
despite / in spite of + noun or -ingNever despite ofDespite the evidence, he denied it.
Granted, / Admittedly, / I grant you that…One-off concession, followed by "but" or a turnGranted, the data are thin; even so, the trend is clear.
Even so / All the same / NonethelessConnectors between sentencesThe plan is flawed. Even so, it is better than nothing.
  • albeit is not a free synonym of although: it is used with a reduced phrase (albeit slowly, albeit tired). With a full subject and verb, use although / though.
  • Be that as it may is not a real concession but a transition: "I'll leave it there and move on". It is one of the most useful and most imitated formulas in formal speech.
  • Contrast vs. concession: whereas / while contrast two facts (Whereas Ana speaks first, Luis prefers to listen); although / even though / much as concede.
  • Argumentative direction: the conceded information comes first or between commas; the thesis goes in the main clause. If you reverse the order, you change what seems important.

watch.wrong: Despite of the evidence, he denied it.
watch.right: Despite the evidence, he denied it.
watch.why: "Despite" takes no "of"; with "of" you say "in spite of".

watch.wrong: Albeit he was tired, he kept speaking.
watch.right: Though he was tired, he kept speaking.
watch.why: "Albeit" is used with a reduced phrase (albeit tired), not with a full subject and verb.

watch.wrong: However she is talented, she doesn't work hard.
watch.right: However talented she is, she doesn't work hard.

watch.wrong: Be that as it may be, we must go on.
watch.right: Be that as it may, we must go on.
watch.why: The formula is fixed: Be that as it may.

learn.title: The subjunctive: mandative, 'were' and fixed formulas
learn.html:
English keeps living remnants of the subjunctive, especially in formal register and in the language of debates, minutes and laws. They are short, but very revealing of level.

1. Mandative subjunctive: after verbs and adjectives of demand, recommendation or necessity, the verb takes the base form (no -s, be for to be, no do in the negative).

TriggerExample
demand, insist, propose, recommend, suggest, require, urge, request, orderThe board demanded that she resign. / I suggest that he not speak first.
essential, vital, crucial, imperative, important, necessary, desirableIt is essential that every member be informed. / It is vital that nobody leave early.
  • Negative: that he not speak (not doesn't).
  • British alternative: should + infinitive (that she should resign) or, more informally, the indicative (that she resigns). The pure subjunctive is more common in American English and in formal texts.
  • Nuance: insist with the subjunctive expresses demand (He insisted that I go); with the indicative, it asserts a fact (He insisted that I was wrong). Suggest with the subjunctive means proposing; with the indicative it means "indicate" (The data suggest that he is lying).

2. Were-subjunctive (unreal): If I were you…, I wish it were Friday, as if she were a stranger. In careful register were is kept for all persons; was is common in informal speech.

3. Fixed formulas (learned as blocks): Come what may (whatever happens), Suffice it to say… (it is enough to say…), Be that as it may, So be it, Heaven forbid / God forbid (God forbid), Far be it from me to… (I would never presume to…), Perish the thought (no way), as it were (so to speak), Long live….

watch.wrong: The board demanded that she resigns.
watch.right: The board demanded that she resign.
watch.why: After "demand" comes the base form, without -s: that she resign.

watch.wrong: It is vital that nobody to leave early.
watch.right: It is vital that nobody leave early.
watch.why: In the mandative "to" is not used: straight to the base form.

watch.wrong: Suffice to say, it didn't go well.
watch.right: Suffice it to say, it didn't go well.
watch.why: Fixed formula: Suffice it to say.

learn.title: Parallelism and rhetorical devices
learn.html:
Parallelism consists of repeating the same grammatical structure in elements that perform the same function. It is the backbone of almost all effective rhetoric: it aids tracking, creates rhythm and gives an appearance of logical balance.

DeviceWhat it isOriginal example
TricolonThree parallel elements; the third is usually the strongestWe aim to inform, to persuade and, above all, to inspire.
AnaphoraRepeating the opening of successive sentencesWe will not tire. We will not falter. We will not fail.
AntithesisSetting ideas against each other in a symmetrical structureNot a ceiling but a floor; not a favour but a right.
ChiasmusCrossed structure A-B / B-AWe do not debate to win; we win only when we have debated well.
Rhetorical questionA question whose purpose is to assertIs this the kind of transparency we want?
Correlativesboth… and / either… or / not only… but also / the more… the moreThe more we delay, the more it costs.
  • Golden rule: the elements of a list or a correlative pair have the same form: three infinitives, three gerunds, three adjectives. She likes debating, writing and reading (not debating, to write and reading).
  • Correlatives: what follows each part must be of the same type: not only intelligent but also diligent (adjective + adjective), either we compromise or the talks collapse (clause + clause).
  • Parallel comparatives: the more … the more requires the in both halves.
  • Beware of hollow rhythm: a sentence can sound magnificent and assert nothing. Ask yourself what it actually claims.
  • Intensification: in a tricolon, order from weakest to strongest; in an antithesis, put what you want remembered second.

watch.wrong: She is not only intelligent but also she works hard.
watch.right: She is not only intelligent but also hard-working.
watch.why: "Not only… but also" requires parallel elements: adjective + adjective.

watch.wrong: The proposal is cheap, effective and it is easy to implement.
watch.right: The proposal is cheap, effective and easy to implement.
watch.why: The three elements of the list must be adjectives.

watch.wrong: We must either compromise or the talks will collapse.
watch.right: Either we must compromise or the talks will collapse.
watch.why: "Either… or" connects parallel elements: clause with clause.

watch.wrong: The more we delay, more it costs.
watch.right: The more we delay, the more it costs.
watch.why: The structure is the + comparative, the + comparative.

learn.title: Strategy: refuting with courtesy
learn.html:
A good rebuttal has four moves: (1) acknowledge what is valid, (2) mark the disagreement gently, (3) counter-argue with reason or evidence and (4) steer back to the central point. Attack the argument, never the person.

  • Acknowledge: I take your point. / That's fair as far as it goes. / I'll grant you that.
  • Mark disagreement: …but I wonder whether that's the whole story. / With respect, I'd question… / If I may, I'd push back on…
  • Counter-argue: The evidence points the other way: … / That overlooks the fact that… / The problem with that view is…
  • Steer back: Which brings us back to… / Let's not lose sight of… / The real issue is surely… (with surely you put pressure on the listener: use it with care).
  • To avoid: You're wrong. / That's ridiculous. (direct attack); No, but…; and the typical error of Spanish speakers: I'm not agree (correct: I don't agree).
  • Intonation: lowering both volume and speed when disagreeing sounds firmer than raising the pitch. Courtesy does not reduce force; it sustains it.
  • Paraphrase first: summarising the rival argument to the satisfaction of the person who made it, before refuting it, avoids the straw man and disarms their defence.

learn.title: Phrases for moderating, interrupting and concluding
learn.html:
• Taking the floor: If I might come in here… / May I make a point of information? / If I could just finish my point…
  • Conceding gracefully: Point taken. / I'll grant you that. / I stand corrected. / That's a fair challenge.
  • Disagreeing courteously: With respect, that rather misses the point. / I take your point, but I wonder whether it's the whole story. / I'd respectfully disagree.
  • Diverting without offending: That's somewhat beside the point. / Let's not lose sight of… / Be that as it may…
  • Summarising and closing: To sum up… / All things considered… / Which brings me to my final point.
  • Softening a strong criticism: Far be it from me to criticise, but… / I don't mean to be rude, but… / With the greatest respect,… (note: in British English "with respect" usually announces a serious disagreement).
  • Asking for clarification: What exactly are you driving at? / Could you spell out what you mean?

write.prompt: Persuasive speech of 300 to 400 words for or against the motion: "This house believes that social media has made public debate worse." Open by conceding a point with Much as… or Granted,…, use at least one inverted concessive (Try as…, Brilliant as…), one mandative subjunctive (It is essential that…), a tricolon and an antithesis, and close with a rhetorical question or a formula such as Be that as it may.

A correct mandative subjunctive (It is essential that… be / that she resign)
Impeccable parallelism in lists and correlatives (tricolon, not only… but also)
An explicit rhetorical device (antithesis, anaphora or rhetorical question) and a closing formula such as Be that as it may
write.model:
Madam Speaker, honourable members, I stand in support of the motion.

Much as I admire the connectivity that social media has given us, I cannot pretend that it has improved the way we argue. Granted, it has opened the conversation to millions who were once excluded from it; but access is not the same as quality, and a louder debate is not a better one.

Consider what these platforms reward. They reward speed over thought, outrage over reason, and certainty over curiosity. A considered paragraph is ignored; a cruel one-liner is shared a thousand times. Brilliant as the technology is, it was built to hold our attention, not to inform our judgement, and attention is most easily held by anger.

Try as we might to engage with opponents online, the format works against us. Not only do we meet fewer opposing views, but we are also sorted, silently and efficiently, into communities that agree with us. We came for a public square; we have been given a thousand private echo chambers. The square was crowded and noisy, yes, but it was shared. The echo chamber is crowded and noisy, and it is ours alone.

What, then, should be done? It is essential that platforms be held accountable for what their algorithms amplify. It is vital that every citizen learn to question a source before sharing it. And it is imperative that we, as speakers, insist that our disagreements remain disagreements and never become wars.

Opponents will tell us that debate has always been rough, that pamphlets were once as vicious as posts. They are right, to a point. But pamphlets did not follow us into our pockets, and they did not learn what would enrage us most. Never before has a tool so cheap rewarded cruelty so reliably.

Be that as it may, I do not ask the House to condemn technology. I ask it to be honest about what it has done: it has given everyone a voice, and made almost no one a listener. If we want a public debate worthy of the name, must we not first learn to listen?

I beg to propose.

write.prompt: Written rebuttal of 300 to 400 words to this argument: "Standardised exams are the only fair way to assess students; everything else just rewards charm." Acknowledge what is valid, disagree courteously, set against it evidence or reasoning, and name at least one fallacy (for example, the straw man or the slippery slope) without attacking the person who made the claim.
checklist: Between 300 and 400 words in a formal and courteous tone
An opening acknowledgement (I take your point / I'll grant you that)
A gentle disagreement and a counter-argument with reason or evidence
At least one advanced concessive (Much as…, Be that as it may…, albeit)
One fallacy identified by name and explained
Varied argument verbs (contend, undermine, pre-empt, bolster)
No personal attacks or expressions such as "I'm not agree"
write.model:
I take your point that standardised exams have real virtues, and I will grant you at the outset that they offer something few other methods can: every student answers the same questions, under the same conditions, and is marked by the same criteria. That consistency is not trivial, and I would not wish to dismiss it.

Much as I respect that argument, however, I cannot accept that exams are the only fair way to assess students. You contend that everything else merely rewards charm, but this seems to me a straw man: nobody seriously defending coursework, portfolios or oral assessment claims that students should be graded on personality. Such methods are judged against explicit criteria, moderated by second markers and, albeit imperfectly, designed to measure skills that a timed paper cannot capture, such as sustained research, collaboration and revision. To reduce them to charm is to attack a weaker version of the position than the one actually held, and that is precisely what a straw man does. I raise this not to criticise you, but because the distinction matters for the rest of the debate.

There is also evidence that undermines the claim of exam fairness. Research on test anxiety suggests that the pressure of a single high-stakes sitting disadvantages some capable students, while others benefit from expensive coaching that is not available to everyone. A test may be uniform in procedure and still unequal in effect. Fairness, in other words, is not only a matter of identical conditions; it is a matter of whether those conditions give every candidate a genuine opportunity to show what they know.

Nor does the case for a mixed approach rely on abandoning exams. Examinations can bolster a broader picture of achievement, and a well-designed portfolio can pre-empt the objection that written coursework is easy to outsource. Used together, each method compensates for the weaknesses of the other.

Be that as it may, I suspect we agree on more than it appears: that assessment should be rigorous, transparent and trusted. Where we differ is whether a single instrument can deliver all three. I would argue that it cannot, and that students are better served by several.

reading.title: In defence of losing an argument
reading.intro: Read the essay and answer the questions. Pay attention to the author's position and to the nuances.
paragraphs: There is a moment in almost every heated debate when one speaker realises that the other has a point. The sensible response, it might seem, is to say so. In practice, a surprising number of people do the opposite: they dig their heels in, reach for a louder tone, or change the subject with a flourish. The psychology is well documented. To concede is to risk looking as though you have lost, and in a culture that treats argument as combat, losing feels like a personal failure.

Yet the history of rhetoric suggests that this instinct has things backwards. Classical teachers of oratory did not prize the speaker who never yielded; they prized the one who could state the opposing case so fairly that its own defenders would nod in recognition. Much as modern audiences enjoy a good takedown, the arguments that persuade over time are rarely the ones that humiliate. They are the ones that begin by granting what is true in the other side's position and then explain, patiently, why it is not the whole truth.

Consider the three most common traps. The first is the straw man: restating an opponent's view in a weakened form so that it can be knocked over with ease. The second is the red herring, a dramatic but irrelevant detail introduced to pull the discussion away from where it is going badly. The third, and perhaps the most corrosive, is the ad hominem, in which the speaker attacks the person rather than the point. All three create the impression of victory while leaving the question untouched. Audiences, it turns out, are more discerning than debaters assume. Studies of televised exchanges suggest that viewers quietly mark down a speaker who resorts to such tactics, even when they happen to agree with the conclusion.

The alternative is not meekness. A good rebuttal can be courteous and ruthless at once. Try as one might to soften it, 'I take your point, but' is a perfectly firm sentence; its power lies in the order of its parts. Acknowledgement comes first, disagreement second and, ideally, a reason the listener can examine. Formal debating societies train this habit deliberately. At one university club I visited, novices are required to open every reply by summarising the previous speaker's argument to that speaker's satisfaction. Only when the opponent says 'yes, that is what I meant' may the novice proceed to attack it. The rule is tiresome for about a week, and then it changes how members listen for the rest of their lives.

Structure helps, too. Skilled speakers lean on parallelism: three examples, three verbs, a phrase repeated at the head of successive sentences. It is not mere ornament. Repetition gives the listener a framework in which to place each new idea, and a well-built contrast, not a ban but a boundary, not a punishment but a promise, can lodge in the memory long after the evidence has faded. The danger, of course, is that rhythm can disguise thin reasoning. A sentence can sound magnificent and say nothing. The discipline is to ask of any ringing line what, precisely, it claims.

Then there are the conventions of formal speech and writing that survive in the mandative subjunctive: it is essential that the chair be impartial; the committee requested that each member submit a statement. These forms sound old-fashioned to some ears, yet they signal exactly what the debating chamber values: procedure, restraint and respect for the rules that keep disagreement productive. Be that as it may, no rule can replace the willingness to be moved.

Which brings us back to the concession. The best debaters I have watched are not those who never lose a point, but those who lose points gracefully and visibly, so that the points they hold carry more weight. 'I was wrong about that' is a short sentence, and it is remarkably expensive to say. Perhaps that is exactly why it persuades.

listening.title: The motion before the house
listening.intro: Listen to an excerpt from a university debate. You can repeat it.

lines.text: Order, order. We now come to the main motion: 'This house believes that politicians should be required to publish their private emails.' Imogen, you have the floor for four minutes.
Thank you, Madam Chair. Much as I respect the right to privacy, I contend that public office changes the terms. Citizens aren't asking for gossip; they're asking for accountability.
Transparency isn't a luxury; it's a condition of trust. And trust, once lost, can't be legislated back.
Thank you. Tariq, for the opposition.

Thank you, Madam Chair. I take the proposer's point about trust, I really do. But let's be clear about what she's actually asking for. Every message, every draft, every awkward joke on the public record?

Be that as it may on transparency, the likely result is that officials will simply stop writing anything down. Is that the accountability we want? Or will decisions just move to phone calls that leave no trace?
Not just now, thank you. Let me finish this thought.
It is essential that we distinguish between the public record and the private person. Try as I might to see a workable line, I can't find one in this motion.
Might I say, with respect, that the member is attacking a version of the motion that nobody proposed? We said official business, not private life.
I'll allow that. Tariq, you may respond.
Fair enough. The proposer has narrowed her claim, and I concede that official correspondence is a different matter. Even so, the burden of proof still lies with her.
Thank you both. Let's turn now to the floor.
And may I just say that, for all our disagreements, that was a thoroughly enjoyable exchange.
